prompt: Compare a value-based price with a cost-plus price.

task.prompt: An automation project will save a client about $400,000 a year. Delivery cost is $50,000. Your cost-plus policy targets a 40% gross margin. A value-based approach would price at 25% of the first year's saving.

fields.label: Gross margin at the value-based price

task.explanation: Cost-plus = 50,000 ÷ 0.6 = $83333.33. Value-based = 25% × 400,000 = $100000, a 50% margin, while the client still keeps three-quarters of the first year's value. Value pricing needs a credible, client-agreed estimate of the value.

prompt: Position price in a market racing to the bottom.

task.prompt: In a segment you target, several competitors quote 30–40% below your rates. Your win rate there has fallen.

steps.question: What is the best strategic response?
options: Look at win/loss data to see where you lose, then sharpen positioning on outcomes and offer a lower-scope entry option
Cut rates across the board by 35%
Exit the segment immediately
Match each competitor quote deal by deal
steps.explanation: Blanket cuts destroy margin everywhere; understand why you lose and compete on value with a scoped entry point.

steps.question: Data shows you still win when clients care about long-term maintenance. What follows?
options: Ignore the finding
Target and message to clients for whom long-term quality matters, and qualify out pure price shoppers earlier
Lower prices for those clients too
Stop offering maintenance
steps.explanation: Pricing strategy includes choosing which buyers to serve.

prompt: Rank pricing approaches by value captured.

task.prompt: For a project with a clearly quantified, client-agreed ROI, rank these pricing approaches from most to least value captured by the agency.

items.label: Value-based price tied to the agreed ROI
Tiered options (good, better, best) anchored on value

task.explanation: When value is clear and agreed, pricing from it captures the most. Cost-plus ignores value; matching the lowest bid gives away both value and margin.

prompt: Find the problems in this discounting policy.

task.prompt: Mark the lines in this draft discounting policy that will hurt pricing discipline.

segments.text: Any discount needs a recorded reason and something received in return.
Sales reps may give up to 25% off without approval.
segments.issue: A high self-approved limit invites routine discounting; approval levels should scale with size.

segments.text: Discounts above 10% need the head of sales; above 15%, the CEO.
End-of-quarter discounts of 20% are automatically available to close deals.
segments.issue: Predictable quarter-end discounts teach clients to wait.

segments.text: Discounts are applied to the rate card, never to estimates.
Discount levels are not tracked after the deal closes.
segments.issue: Without tracking, you cannot see how discounting affects margin.

prompt: Work out how much volume a price increase can afford to lose.

task.prompt: You plan to raise your hourly rate from $50 to $55. Your delivery cost is $32 an hour.

fields.label: Maximum share of hours you can lose and keep the same gross profit

task.explanation: Profit per hour rises from $18 to $23. You keep the same profit at 78.26% of today's hours (18 ÷ 23), so you can lose up to 21.74% of volume. A 10% price rise rarely loses that much.

prompt: Choose how to price AI usage in a proposal.

task.prompt: A client wants a fixed price for an AI support assistant, including model API costs, but cannot predict usage.

steps.question: Which pricing structure best balances risk?
options: Fixed price for the build; AI usage billed as pass-through or in usage tiers with caps
One fixed price covering everything for three years
Free AI usage to win the deal
Usage billed at a large unexplained markup
steps.explanation: Usage-driven costs belong in usage-based pricing; a fixed price turns your margin into a bet on adoption.

steps.question: What must the proposal state for this to work?
options: Only the model name
The usage assumptions, how usage is measured and reported, and what happens above the tier
Nothing; keep it simple
That costs will never change
steps.explanation: Written assumptions and reporting turn later conversations into a reference to what was agreed.

options: Pricing at cost plus a fixed margin
Charging whatever competitors charge
Setting the price from the measurable value to the client rather than from your cost
Giving discounts to high-value clients
mcq.explanation: It works when value is quantified and agreed with the client.

prompt: Why offer three tiered options (for example good, better, best) in a proposal?

options: To confuse the client
Because clients always choose the cheapest
To avoid writing a scope
They anchor the conversation on value and let the client choose scope rather than haggle on price
mcq.explanation: Options shift the question from "whether and how much" to "which one", and protect your rate.

prompt: What is the main risk of frequent ad-hoc discounting?

options: It erodes margins and teaches clients your list price is negotiable
It shortens sales cycles too much
It makes invoices more complex
It increases win rates too much
mcq.explanation: Discount discipline protects both margin and price credibility.
